'''Courage''' was an English [[brewery]], founded by John Courage in [[London|London, England]], in 1787.

==History==
===Origin and family ownership===
{{overly detailed|section|date=May 2025}}
The Courage Brewery was started by John Courage (1 October 1761 – October 1797).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Courage Brewery – History |url=https://couragebeers.co.uk/history/ |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=Courage Beers}}</ref><ref name=":15" /><ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Brooks |first=Jay |title=Historic Beer Birthday: John Courage (copied from old John Courage website takecourage.info) |url=https://brookstonbeerbulletin.com/historic-beer-birthday-john-courage/ |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=brookstonbeerbulletin.com}}</ref> He was a Scottish shipping agent believed to be of [[French Huguenot]] descent hailing from Aberdeen,<ref name=":0" /> although other sources suggest his family may have originated from Flanders, as there were no records of French Huguenot immigration to Aberdeen and there was a stronger tradition of brewing in that region.<ref name=":9"/>

John Courage moved to London in or about 1780 to become an agent for the Glasgow shipping firm of Carron. His work was located at Glasgow Wharf (just downstream from the [[Tower of London]]). From his workplace, he could see the brewing operations in Southwark which encouraged him to diversify his interests into the brewing industry.<ref name=":0" />

On 20 December 1787,<ref name=":15">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.S. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |page=8 |language=English}}</ref> John Courage, together with a group of friends purchased the [[Anchor Brewhouse]] in [[Horsleydown]], [[Bermondsey]], from John and Hagger Ellis <ref name=":9" /> for £615 13s.11d.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Richard Courage obituary (extract from Daily Telegraph 15 September 1994) |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php?title=Richard_Courage |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=Brewery History}}</ref>
[[File:Portrait of John Courage. Founder of Courage Brewery (1787-1793).jpg|left|thumb|Portrait of John Courage (1761–1797)<ref name=":20">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |date=1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |location=Victoria, London}}</ref>]]

John Courage died suddenly at the age of 36 in 1797 and was buried at St. John's, [[Horsleydown]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":9" /> In 1786, he had married Harriot (née Stewart or Murdoch) (1765–1797/98)<ref name=":9"/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.S. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |year=1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd|location=Victoria London |page=7 |language=English}}</ref> and the couple had four children, John (Junior), Ann, Elisabeth and Harriet <ref name=":9" /> On John's death, his wife took over the running of the business until her own death.<ref name=":0" />

Since the four Courage children were still young (the eldest, John, was only 9 years old at the time of Harriet's death), John Donaldson, the Managing Clerk, took over running the day-to-day business and care for the children.<ref name=":9" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.S. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |year=1932 |location=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd. Victoria, London |page=9 |language=English}}</ref> In 1800, John Donaldson was named a partner and the business was renamed Courage & Donaldson reflecting the effective partnership.<ref name=":0" />   Profits were initially split with Donaldson receiving a third, which was subsequently amended to half of profits and half of the capital of the business.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":16">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.S. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |page=11 |language=English}}</ref>
John Courage Junior (26 June 1788 – 8 March 1854)<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":16" /> joined the business in 1804 at the age of 14 and became a partner in the business in 1811.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Brooks |first=Jay |date=2024 |title=Historic Beer Birthday: John Courage Jr. (referencing old Courage website takecourage.info) |url=https://brookstonbeerbulletin.com/historic-beer-birthday-john-courage-jr/ |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=brookstonbeerbulletin.com}}</ref> John the Second married Susan, the daughter of a Norfolk brewer, Sidney Hawes of Coltishall in 1823. The Courages lived at De Crespigny Terrace, Camberwell and had ten children.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.S |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |page=9 |language=English}}</ref>

In  1836 John Donaldson retired from the business and his share was transferred to his son Thomas  and his brother Robert joined in 1841. In 1851, the Donaldson family withdrew from management.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":16" />

In 1852, John Courage Junior and his sons Robert and John (the third) (25 January 1829 – 1861) then took over the business in partnership.<ref name=":16" />  On John Courage Junior's death, the sons carried on, and in 1856 a further partnership was formed when John (the third) and Robert (1830–1894) admitted Edward (1833–1904) into the partnership. Following John (the third)'s death, the partnership was reconstituted again, when Henry Courage was admitted. One final change to the partnership was made in 1882 with the admission of Robert's son, Robert Michell Courage (died 1887).<ref name=":10" /><ref name=":17">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1787–1932) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |date=1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |location=Victoria, London |page=12 |language=English}}</ref>

Robert Courage acted as Chairman of the limited company between 1888 and 1894 followed on his death by Edward Courage who acted as Chairman from 1894 to 1904.<ref name=":18" /> Edward Courage resided for nearly all his life at Shenfield Place, Shenfield, Essex. Having entered the business in 1856, he became a partner in 1889.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Partner 1897–1927) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Haskell Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |pages=27–33 |language=English}}</ref> 
Following the death of Edward Courage, he was followed as Chairman by his son, [[Old Etonian]] Raymond Courage (1866–1951), [[Lord of the manor]] [[Edgcote|of Edgcote]] from 1926 until his death.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Burke |first1=Bernard |title=Burke's Landed Gentry |date=1937 |publisher=Burke's Peerage |page=495 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jurmAAAAMAAJ&q=burke%27s+peerage+dorothy+courage+De+Zeote |access-date=24 June 2023 |quote=PAGE 495 ... Raymond Courage [1866–1951] of Edgcote Manor ...COURAGE, of Shenfield Place, Brentwood, Essex, b . 10 July 1832; educ ... BURKE's Peerage) . 1. Helen Beatrice, d . 5 May 1922 . 2. Evelyne ... Dorothy, m . Herman de Zoete ...}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Edgcote House Edgcote, near Banbury Northamptonshire England |url=https://www.thedicamillo.com/house/edgcote-house/ |publisher=Curt DiCamillo. All Rights Reserved. |access-date=14 June 2023 |date=2024 |quote=Edgcote is a nine-bay two-story house erected between 1747 and 1752 for London merchant Richard Chauncey. Built of local ironstone with gray stone dressings, the interior is notable for its Chinese style drawing room. Edgcote House, together with 1,700 acres, was sold in June 2005 by Christopher Courage (of the brewing family) for £30 million. Edgcote is possibly most notable today as Netherfield, the country seat of Mr. Bingley, in the BBC's 1995 production of "Pride and Prejudice."...Courage family here 1926–2005.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=The Market: Mystery buyer lands £30m country pile |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/the-market-mystery-buyer-lands-pound30m-country-pile-wlp3nb7snrh |access-date=13 June 2023 |publisher=The Times (UK) |date=30 October 2005 |quote=Edgcote was sold by Christopher Courage, 43, scion of the brewing dynasty [as son of Edward Raymond Courage (1906–1982) and grandson of Raymond Courage (1866–1951)], who was born there and had lived there all his life. Courage and his .}}</ref><ref name="UK Daily Telegraph">{{cite web |last1=Ward |first1=V. |title=Aristocratic roots of Peter Phillips' NHS nurse girlfriend revealed |work=The Telegraph |date=22 June 2024 |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/royal-family/2024/06/22/peter-phillips-nhs-nurse-girlfriend-harriet-sperling-ascot/ |access-date=25 June 2024 |publisher=UK Daily Telegraph}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025 |title=Edgcote House Edgcote, near Banbury Northamptonshire England |url=https://www.thedicamillo.com/house/edgcote-house/ |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=Curt DiCamillo. All Rights Reserved.}}</ref> Raymond Courage was the great-grandson of John Courage.<ref name=":1" />

Raymond Courage was succeeded by his son, Richard Courage (1913–1994), as Chairman of the company throughout the 1950s to the 1970s.<ref name=":1" />

===Incorporation and expansion of the business (1888 – World War II)===

With London's population growing from around 1 million in 1800 to around 6.9 million in 1900,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Why Did London's Population Growth from 1800 to 1900 |url=https://www.ncesc.com/geographic-pedia/why-did-londons-population-growth-from-1800-to-1900/ |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=ncesc.com/Geographic-pedia|date=19 February 2025 }}</ref> demand for beer in the city grew exponentially throughout the century.  By 1887, the annual production ("barrelage") of Courage had reached 300,000 barrels. The growth in the size of the business probably led to Courage & Co. Limited becoming registered as a Limited Liability Company on 28 April 1888, and the company became simply known as "Courage".<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":17" /> On 21 May 1889, Messrs, Prescott, Cave, Buxton, Loder & Co. Ltd. issued a prospectus for floating the company with a total capital of £1.5 million with £0.6 million of debenture stock. In 1897, a further £0.4 million of debenture stock was raised.<ref name=":18">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Partner 1897–1927) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |date=1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd. |location=Victoria, London |pages=27–33 |language=English}}</ref>

[[File:Engraving of Anchor Brewhouse Horsley Down.jpg|left|thumb|Engraving of Anchor Brewhouse <ref name=":20" />]]
As with many other brewers, the Company initially operated as a supplier of [[Pub|public houses]] rather than owning a significant estate of its own. The public houses were owned by the licensed victualler ("landlord") who would often raise capital from brewery companies in order to finance the purchase through the provision of a loan backed by a mortgage on the property. As a condition of the loan, Courage would stipulate interest rates, repayment rates and have an exclusive supply arrangement to provide its range of beers to the public house, securing the loan with a first mortgage on the property.  The landlord would be free to then arrange loans and contracts with suppliers of [[Pale ale|Pale Ale]] (which Courage could not produce in London) and liquors who would provide further loans and take second and third charges on the property. The balance of the cost of the public house would be provided by the landlord's own capital.  In 1890, the value of loans on Courage's [[balance sheet]] was £1,654,355 compared to the value of self-owned public houses of £221,602.<ref name=":21">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787-1932 |publisher=Jordan-Haskell Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |pages=24–26 |language=English}}</ref>

The late 1890s represented a boom time for the breweries. The availability of cheap money led to increased competition for the purchase of houses pushing up purchase prices. By 1897, the value of the company's loan book had grown to £2,202,879 and self-owned public houses to £786,071.<ref name=":21" />

From the peak in 1897, the business underwent a transformation with a significant decline in loans and commensurate growth in Courage's direct ownership of the estate. In addition, a downturn in public house prices after a boom in the 1890s led to many landlords defaulting on their loans which reverted to the first mortgage holder or became available for purchase at lower prices. The purchase of public houses was made possible by the availability of cheap equity and debt finance to Courage based on security provided by the ownership of its own estate of public houses. By 1931, the company's business model had been completely reversed with the value of the loan book being £333,897 and self-owned public houses to £2,695,672.<ref name=":21" />

A fire at the Anchor Brewhouse on 5 May 1891 destroyed the building which required the rebuilding and all brewing ceased for a month with beer being purchased from Barclay, Perkins & Co. to supply its public houses.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.S. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |date=1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |location=Victoria, London |page=15}}</ref> The Anchor Brewhouse concentrated on production of mild ale and stout suited to the quality of water available from its wells. However, the water did not have the mineral ingredients needed for pale ale. Therefore, pale ale production was subcontracted to Flower & Sons Ltd (1872–1886) and then Fremlins Ltd (1886–1903).<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Courage and Co. Limited Acquisition and Closure Trail |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php?title=Courage_%26_Co._Ltd_-_Acquisition_and_Closure_Trail |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=Brewery History}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Alton Brewery Co |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Alton_Brewery_Co |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=Brewery History}}</ref>

From the start of the 20th century, Courage went through a period of expansion through acquisition which saw Courage buy seven breweries and their associated licensed public houses.<ref name=":0" /> As with other brewers, these purchases focused on the expanding the number of tied public houses whilst nearly all of the acquired breweries were closed down within a couple of years of becoming part of the Courage group.<ref>{{Cite web |date=6 January 2024 |title=Courage & Co. Ltd - Acquisition and Closure Trail |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Courage_%26_Co._Ltd_-_Acquisition_and_Closure_Trail |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref>
[[File:Courage's Alton Brewery and rail siding c.1930.jpg|thumb|Courage's Alton Brewery and rail siding c.1930 <ref name=":20" />]]

The acquisitions started with the purchase of the Alton Brewery Co. (formerly called Halls Brewery until 1899), located in Turks Street, [[Alton, Hampshire]], and its 77 tied houses in February 1903.<ref name=":2" /> The facility initially replaced the pale ale produced by Fremlins Ltd <ref name=":2" /> but expanded as further acquisitions were made and the estate of tied public houses grew.

Courage then made further acquisitions in London, Surrey, Kent and Berkshire expanding its geographical presence into surrounding areas that could easily be supplied by its two breweries in London and Alton.<ref name=":2" />

The purchases included the Camden Brewery, consisting of freehold premises and 78 public houses in the North-West of London where the company had little presence and Courage Beers were virtually unknown.  The Brewery was subsequently closed in 1926.<ref name=":19">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Partner 1897–1927) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |pages=38–44 |language=English}}</ref>

Farnham United Breweries was acquired in 1927. The brewery was situated close to Alton and had its own maltings and a holding of 196 licensed houses with an annual output of 45,000 barrels. As it could easily be supplied and managed from Alton the Farnham brewery itself was closed down. The Alton Brewery was extended to increase capacity to supply the acquired licensed houses. Courage raised further equity of £0.4 million to pay for the purchase <ref name=":19" />

In  March 1930, Courage acquired Noakes & Company in Bermondsey. The property consisted of the Brewery and 120  public houses around Bermondsey. and the Nevile Reid Brewery  in [[Windsor, Berkshire]] with 140 public houses. Further in 1920, Noakes & Co. had purchased the Royal Brewery, Windsor of J. Canning & Son and 20 public houses. Courage raised further debt of £0.4 million to pay for the purchase.<ref name=":19" />

In 1931, Courage's estate consisted of 886 public houses of which 462 were in London with 273 in Hampshire /Surrey and 140 in Windsor and Slough.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.N |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskill Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |pages=45–51 |language=English}}</ref>
[[File:The Grove Hotel, Dulwich, London c.1930.jpg|left|thumb|The Grove Hotel, Dulwich, London c.1930 <ref name=":20" />]]
In 1921, the Licensing Act was passed. This prohibited the sale of beer and liquors for more than 9 hours a day in London and 8 1/2 hours elsewhere. This precipitated a drinking "rush hour" and existing public houses were considered too small to cope with the concentration of demand into a limited number of hours. Courage's utilized its in-house building department consisting of surveyors, draughts men and tradesmen to enlarge and reconfigure its existing public house estate. The Tudor style of house was taken as the template for rebuilding and the first significant structure to be redeveloped was the "Grove Tavern", Lordship Lane, Dulwich, famous for once being Lord Byron's residence.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Haskell |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |pages=45–49 |language=English}}</ref>  The Grove Tavern is now derelict having been destroyed in a fire in 2012. The pub is currently leased by Stonegate but owned by the Dulwich Estate. It is anticipated that the site will be demolished when the lease ends in September 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davison |first=Emily |date=10 February 2025 |title=The Grove pub Dulwich: Uncertain future as lease set to end |url=https://www.newsshopper.co.uk/news/24915651.seo-grove-pub-dulwich-uncertain-future-lease-set-end/ |access-date=15 May 2025 |website=newsshopper.co.uk}}</ref>

Whilst building the Grove Tavern, Courage's also procured a sports ground on adjoining land, which included cricket and football grounds, hard and grass courts for tennis, and a bowling green. The company also provided transport from the brewery in Bermondsey to the ground.'''<ref name=":20" />''' Given its location, this ground is likely to be that currently occupied by Streatham and Marlborough Cricket Club. Courage's provided similar sports facilities in Alton which were redeveloped into residential properties in 2015 and also in Reading from the early 1960s in [[Coley Park]]. The ground was closed in the 1980s. The old site of the ground includes a public park called "Courage Park" named to commemorate its former ownership.
[[File:The Brockley Jack, Brockley, London c.1930.jpg|thumb|The Brockley Jack, Brockley, London <ref name=":20" />]]
Other redevelopments included the Railway Tavern, Station Approach, Catford (now the "Catford Bridge Tavern" owned by Portobello Brewery);<ref>{{Cite web |title=Catford Tavern |url=https://catfordtavern.com/ |access-date=15 May 2025 |website=Catfordtavern.com}}</ref> the Beehive, Beehive Lane, Ilford (now a Harvester)<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Beehive Ilford |url=https://www.harvester.co.uk/restaurants/london/thebeehiveilford?utm_source=bing&utm_medium=organic#/ |access-date=15 May 2025 |website=harvester.co.uk}}</ref> and the Brockley Jack, Brockley Road, Brockley, London a former haunt of Dick Turpin (now run by [[Greene King]]).<ref name=":22" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Brockley Jack |url=https://www.greeneking.co.uk/pubs/greater-london/brockley-jack |access-date=15 May 2025 |website=greeneking.co.uk}}</ref> Redevelopment of public houses extended to the company's public houses in Hampshire/Surrey and Berkshire areas including The Swan Hotel in Alton, Hampshire, (now run by Greene King) the Bush Hotel in Farnham, Surrey (a luxury hotel) the Otter at Ottershaw, Surrey (Miller & Carter Steakhouse) and the George at Wraysbury, Berkshire, (now a steakhouse) all of which are still active public houses and Hotels.<ref name=":22" />

During the pre-World War II era, the company provided its employees with a number of benefits and perks. As well as the company's sports clubs and activities, the company arranged a Contributory Superannuation Scheme for staff to secure future pensions dependent on the length of service and salary, and benefits to widows and family in case of the staff member's death. The company also started the Hospital Savings Association to help deal with medical costs. The care for the company's staff was farsighted. In 1926, in the General Strike, Courage reported that not a single man ceased work.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Director 1897–1927) |first=G.N. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |year=1932 |location=Victoria, London |pages=52–54 |language=English}}</ref>

===End of World War II until 1970===

The post war period saw continued growth demand for beer as a result of population growth, an end to post-war austerity and, further improvements in transportation with the advent of motor vehicles. This reinforced the economic forces leading to the consolidation of the brewing industry.

In 1955, Courage and Co. Ltd merged with Barclay, Perkins & Co Ltd. at the nearby [[Anchor Brewery, Southwark|Anchor Brewery]], Southwark to become Courage & Barclay Ltd.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Grace's Guide To British Industrial History - Barclay, Perkins and Co. |url=https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/Barclay,_Perkins_and_Co |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=gracesguide.co.uk}}</ref>  At this stage, Courage & Barclay Ltd had approximately 1,250 tied houses within the estate, consolidating Courage's presence in London.<ref name=":2" /> The Anchor Brewery was closed and the site converted into a bottling and packing plant.<ref name=":1" />

In 1960, Courage & Barclay Ltd acquired the [[Reading, Berkshire|Reading]] based [[H & G Simonds Ltd]], and the company name was changed to Courage, Barclay, Simonds & Co. Ltd.<ref name=":0" />

In 1961, Georges & Co. Limited  ("[[Georges Bristol Brewery]]") was acquired, based in Bristol with 1,459 tied houses. The brewery and tied houses were referred to as Courage (Western) Ltd. for a while.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Bristol Brewery Georges & Co. Ltd |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Bristol_Brewery_Georges_%26_Co._Ltd |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Grace's Guide To British Industrial History - George's Brewery |url=https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/George's_Brewery |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=gracesguide.co.uk}}</ref>

In 1967, Hole & Co. Ltd, Castle Brewery, Newark-on-Trent, Nottinghamshire was taken over consisting of 220 tied houses.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Hole & Co. Ltd |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php?title=Hole_%26_Co._Ltd |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Grace's Guide To British Industrial History - James Hole & Co |url=https://www.gracesguide.co.uk/James_Hole_and_Co |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=gracesguide.co.uk}}</ref>

The acquisitions extended Courage's business into South Wales, South West England, the East Midlands and South Yorkshire whilst increasing brewing capacity to meet anticipated greater demand. In addition, Courage's made further acquisitions in its existing territory around London and the surrounding area with purchases in Berkshire, Oxfordshire, Middlesex and Essex.<ref name=":2" />

Consumer tastes began to change during this period. In the 1950s, UK brewers had realized the potential of a developing market for lagers. Guinness, an Irish brewing company, began to develop its own product, [[Harp Lager]].  Late in 1960, Guinness decided it needed a joint venture with other breweries in order to give it regional coverage for Harp Lager and enlisted the help of Courage & Barclay Ltd (for the South of England), Scottish and Newcastle breweries (for the North) and Mitchells and Butlers (for the Midlands) between them providing national coverage. As a consequence of entering into this joint venture a new brewing facility was planned for Alton at Manor Park next to the existing facility in Turk Street.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=The Story of the Manor Park Brewery |url=https://www.breweryhistory.com/journal/archive/176/Manor%20Park.pdf |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=Breweryhistory.com}}</ref>

By the late 1960s, the group had assets of approximately £100m, and operated six breweries in London, Reading, Alton (two including the Harp Lager joint venture), Bristol and Newark-on-Trent. It owned 5,000 licensed premises in Southern England, South Wales, the East Midlands and South Yorkshire, employed 15,000 people and produced around {{convert|75|e6impgal|L}} of beer annually.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Index |url=http://takecourage.info/index.html |access-date=22 October 2021 |website=Takecourage.info}} {{Dead link|date=May 2025}}</ref>
[[File:John Smiths Brewery, Tadcaster - geograph.org.uk - 1857346.jpg|left|thumb|John Smith's Brewery Tadcaster]]
In 1970, the name of the company was simplified from Courage, Barclay, Simonds & Co. Ltd to Courage Ltd'<ref name=":0" />  Courage Ltd reached its pinnacle with the acquisition of John Smith's Tadcaster Brewery Co. Ltd ("John Smiths"), located in Tadcaster, South Yorkshire, with about 1,800 tied houses and breweries in Tadcaster and Barnsley.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=John Smith's Tadcaster Brewery Co. Ltd |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/John_Smith%27s_Tadcaster_Brewery_Co._Ltd |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref> By this time John Smith's owned around 1,800 licensed premises throughout the north of England, and as far south as Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire and parts of Cambridgeshire and Shropshire. The merged company held [[asset]]s worth £137 million. By combining Courage's strength in the South of England, and John Smith's in the North, a national brewing company was created. Following the acquisition of John Smiths, Courage had become the fifth largest brewer in the United Kingdom with an estate over 6,000 tied houses.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6" />

In December 1970 Courage Ltd. further acquired Plymouth Breweries Ltd, located in Plymouth, Devon for £6.5 million.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Plymouth Breweries Limited |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Plymouth_Breweries_Ltd |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref>

===Consolidation and the sale of the business===

The 1970s were a difficult decade for the brewing industry.<ref name=":1" /> A downturn in consumption as consumer tastes changed, an economic downturn and a number of strikes among workers had begun to affect revenues. Having anticipated continuing growth, Courage had committed to develop the new "mega-keggery" at Worton Grange in Reading to increase capacity and consolidate production. Construction had quickly got out of control and estimated costs had increased from £28 million to £63 million. In light of these pressures, Richard Courage, the Chairman of Courage Ltd, sold the company to Imperial Tobacco (subsequently called "Imperial Group") for £320 million in 1972.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />  Following the purchase, the name of the company was changed to Imperial Brewing and Leisure Limited.<ref name=":0" />

Courage operated nine breweries in 1970 (London, Alton (two including the Harp Lager facility), Reading, Newark-upon-Trent, Bristol, Tadcaster, Barnsley and Plymouth. The Worton Grange brewery opened in 1978. This led to the centralization of brewing activity at the facility, setting off a substantial round of closures and sale of the existing older facilities.

Brewing continued to be the major industry in Alton throughout the 1970s, despite the development of a light industrial estate on the south side of the railway line.  The town was hard hit by the news that Courage intended to discontinue operations in the town and move to Reading. On the 25 September 1979, the Courage site, the Manor Park ("Harp Lager") facility, sports facility on Anstey Road, pump/well and old maltings were purchased by [[Bass Brewery|Bass Brewing Company ("Bass")]].<ref name=":3" />  The Turk Street brewery was closed by Bass and turned into a bottling and packing facility. It was subsequently closed and the site sold for development. It is now occupied by a Sainsbury Supermarket. Brewing continued in the town until May 2015, when the old Harp Lager facility was closed by its then owners, Molson Coors with the loss of 105 jobs.<ref name=":3" /> In 2025, the Manor Park is being redeveloped for housing.
[[File:Anchor Brewhouse, London.jpg|left|thumb|Anchor Brewhouse]]
The [[Anchor Brewhouse]] in London closed in 1981 as did the bottling and packing facility at The [[Anchor Brewery, Southwark]]. The [[Anchor Brewhouse]] was converted into apartments. 
[[File:Simmonds brewery malthouse - geograph.org.uk - 1329415.jpg|thumb|Simmonds Brewery Malthouse Reading]]
The Bridge Street Brewery, in Reading, Berkshire was acquired with the 1960 purchase of H & G Simonds Ltd. The Reading Brewery became known as Courage (Central) Ltd. It ceased operations in 1979 with all operations transferred to nearby Worton Grange on the outskirts of the town. The Bridge Street brewery was demolished in 1983, with the site redeveloped to become the Oracle shopping centre.<ref>{{Cite web |title=H & G Simonds Ltd |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Simonds_Ltd |access-date=6 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref>

The Plymouth Brewery became known as "Courage South West" for a while. The brewery was closed in March 1984.<ref name=":5" />

The John Smiths Tadcaster Brewery was substantially redeveloped and expanded throughout 1974.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Pudney |first=John |title=A draught of contentment: the story of the Courage Group |date=1971 |publisher=New English Library |isbn=978-0-450-00994-5 |location=London}}</ref> However, the John Smiths Barnsley brewery was closed on 27 March 1976.<ref name=":7" />

By 1986, brewing activity had been consolidated to three sites at Worton Grange in Reading, Tadcaster and Bristol.

===1986 onwards===

In 1986, Hanson Trust acquired the Imperial Group, including Imperial Brewing and Leisure Limited for £2.5 billion. Much of the purchase price came from the sale of what Hanson Trust considered non-core assets and Courage was sold for £1.4 billion to [[Elders Limited|Elders IXL]], an Australian brewing and agribusiness and became part of the Elders Brewing Group.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Saunders |first=Pat |date=2005 |title=Giants, Evolution and Over Regulation in Brewing |url=https://breweryhistory.com/journal/archive/120/bh-120-002.htm |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref>

The Elders Brewing Group were renamed the Fosters Brewing Group in 1990.<ref name=":0" />

In March 1991, Courage acquired the Webster's Brewery, the Ruddles Brewery and Watney's [[Mortlake Brewery|Mortlake Stag Brewery]] from Grand Metropolitan in a deal that pooled 8,450 pubs into the jointly owned Inntrepreneur Estates Company giving each company 50% ownership. Inntrepreneur had to have 4,350 [[tied pub]]s by the time the [[Beer Orders]] took effect, which led to many being sold and fewer being let on [[Tied house|free-of-tie]] leases.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shepherd |first=John |date=30 September 1992 |title=Inntrepreneur brewing up buyout |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/inntrepreneur-brewing-up-buyout-1554789.html |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=The Independent}}</ref>

The Webster's Brewery was closed in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Webster & Sons Ltd |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Webster_%26_Sons_Ltd |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref>

The Ruddles Brewery was sold to Grolsch in 1992, In 1997, Grolsch, in turn, sold Ruddles Brewery to Morland & Co. Ltd. Morland & Co. Ltd closed the brewery in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ruddles Brewery Ltd |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Ruddles_Brewery_Ltd |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref>
[[File:2023-09-15 Facade to the river Avon of the listed building of the 1788 founded Bristol Brewery Georges' & Co. Ltd., Bath Street, Bristol.jpg|thumb|Facade of the Bristol Brewery - George's & Co.Ltd]]
Watney's [[Mortlake Brewery|Mortlake Stag Brewery]] site was sold on to ABinBev in 2002. The site was closed for redevelopment in 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Watney's Mortlake Stag Brewery |url=https://www.londonremembers.com/sites/watney-s-mortlake-stag-brewery |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=londonremembers.com}}</ref>

The Bristol brewery ceased operation in 1999. Some buildings remain but most of the brewery site has been redeveloped for housing and commercial uses.<ref name=":4" />

In 2007, brewing, marketing and sales rights of the Courage brands, Courage Directors, Mild, Light Ale and Best were sold to [[Wells & Young's Brewery|Wells & Young]] of [[Bedford]], which subsequently reverted to Charles Wells, when Wells bought Young's shares of the joint venture. The owners subsequently rekindled production of the famous 10% abv bottled Courage Imperial Russian Stout which was first brewed in the 18th century by Thrale's brewery;.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Courage Imperial Russian Stout Launched | News | Wells and Young's Brewing Company |url=http://www.wellsandyoungs.co.uk/home/news/courage-imperial-russian-stout |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20130505110540/http://www.wellsandyoungs.co.uk/home/news/courage-imperial-russian-stout |archive-date=2013-05-05 |access-date=22 October 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Milner |first=Mark |date=17 January 2007 |title=Courage beers to switch breweries after brand sale |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2007/jan/18/12 |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=theguardian.com}}</ref> These rights were managed by Courage Brands Ltd.<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 January 2007 |title=Wells and Youngs Buy Courage Brands – Wells & Young's Brewing Company Ltd |url=http://www.wellsandyoungs.co.uk/wellsandyoungs/news/wells-and-youngs-and-courage |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070125223306/http://www.wellsandyoungs.co.uk/wellsandyoungs/news/wells-and-youngs-and-courage |archive-date=2007-01-25 |access-date=22 October 2021}}</ref>  [[Scottish & Newcastle]] (and subsequently Heineken) had a 17 per cent stake in Courage Brands Ltd until 2011, when Charles Wells took full ownership.  In 2017, [[Marston's Brewery]] acquired the rights to the Courage brands as part of its acquisition of Charles Wells's Eagle Brewery.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 May 2017 |title=Charles Wells' Bedford brewery sells to Marston's for £55m |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-beds-bucks-herts-39959394 |access-date=22 October 2021 |website=Bbc.co.uk}}</ref>  In 2020, Marston's merged its brewing business with Carlsberg UK (the United Kingdom arm of [[Carlsberg Group]]), in a joint venture valued at £780m. Marston's took a 40% stake and received up to £273m in cash. The deal involved Marston's six breweries and distribution depots, but not its 1,400 pubs.<ref>{{Cite news |date=22 May 2020 |title=Marston's and Carlsberg UK announce £780m merger |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-52770262 |access-date=2020-05-23 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Davies |first1=Rob |date=22 May 2020 |title=Brewers Carlsberg UK and Marston's announce merger |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2020/may/22/beer-brewers-carlsberg-and-marstons-announce-uk-merger |access-date=23 May 2020 |website=The Guardian}}</ref> The merger was approved by the [[Competition and Markets Authority]] on 9 October 2020.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pugh |first1=James |date=9 October 2020 |title=Regulator approves Carlsberg's £780m joint venture with Marston's |url=https://www.expressandstar.com/news/business/2020/10/09/marstons-and-carlsberg-brewing-merger-to-be-completed-after-getting-cma-approval/ |access-date=9 October 2020 |website=[[Express & Star]] |language=en}}</ref> In 2024, Marston's sold their 40% share in Carlsberg Marston's Brewing Company ("CMBC") to Carlsberg for £206m in order to focus on running the pub business.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Corser |first=John |date=9 July 2024 |title=Beer giant fails to commit to future of Wolverhampton brewery after Marston's sale announced |url=https://www.expressandstar.com/news/business/2024/07/09/future-of-brewing-of-bankss-in-wolverhampton-faces-review/ |website=expressandstar.com}}</ref> The deal to acquire Marston's 40% stake in CMBC was completed on 21 July 2024.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Corser |first1=John |date=31 July 2024 |title=Wolverhampton pubs group Marston's £206m deal completes - full details |url=https://www.expressandstar.com/news/business/2024/07/31/marstons-206m-deal-completes/ |access-date=3 December 2024 |website=Express & Star |language=en}}</ref>

Traditional Courage products have seen a decline in sales in the 21st Century. Courage Best sales have decreased from  421,000 [[hectolitres]] (9.3 million gallons) in 2003 to under 142,000 hectolitres (3.1 million gallons) in 2012.<ref name="ReferenceA">Alcoholic Drinks: Euromonitor from trade sources/national statistics</ref> The Courage Directors has declined to 60,000 hectolitres (1.3 million gallons), from 140,000 hectolitres (3.1 million gallons) in 2003.<ref name="ReferenceA" />

In 2008, brewers Carlsberg and Heineken purchased Scottish & Newcastle for £7.8 billion ($15.3 billion). The assets were split between the two purchasing companies, with the UK assets, including the old remaining Courage breweries, being acquired by Heineken.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 January 2008 |title=Carlsberg and Heineken buy Scottish & Newcastle |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Business/story?id=4195730&page=1 |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=abcnews.go.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Scottish & Newcastle Breweries Ltd |url=https://breweryhistory.com/wiki/index.php/Scottish_%26_Newcastle_Breweries_Ltd |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=breweryhistory.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=26 January 2008 |title=£7.8bn takeover agreed for Scottish & Newcastle |url=https://www.business-live.co.uk/economic-development/78bn-takeover-agreed-scottish--3964760 |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=business-live.co.uk}}</ref>

The Worton Grange (Reading) site was closed in 2010 and became a Tesco Distribution Centre.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=13 February 2008 |title=362 Jobs Lost At Brewery |url=https://www.getreading.co.uk/news/local-news/update-362-jobs-lost-brewery-4255052 |access-date=7 May 2025 |website=getreading.co.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=2008-02-12 |title=Job fears as brewery set to close |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/berkshire/7240491.stm |access-date=2010-04-30 |work=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Reading Courage Brewery shuts down after 30 years |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/berkshire/8600622.stm |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=news.bbc.co.uk|date=2 April 2010 }}</ref>

The Tadcaster brewery remains in operation as part of the Heineken group. It is the only remaining Courage associated brewery still in production.

==Branding and advertising==
===Golden Cockerel===

The Golden Cockerel image is thought to come from the Courage family's coat of arms, a reference back to the probable French Huguenot heritage.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Courage and Co. 1949–1955 |url=https://www.scottbrownrigg.com/company/news/courage-and-co-1949-1955/ |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=scottbrownrigg.com}}</ref> The symbol was used haphazardly within the company for many years on stationery but not standardized. Between 1949 and 1955, Courage appointed Milner Gray of Design Research Unit ("DRU) to develop a corporate identity. Using the golden cockerel as the logo, the image was used on the inside and outside of public houses and breweries and on lorries.

===Slogans===

At the same time as the branding exercise, the company introduced a new slogan. "Take Courage" was commonly printed on company material, beer mats and ashtrays from the 1950s to the 1980s.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |date=15 April 2009 |title=Take Courage' beer advert banned |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/7999250.stm |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=news.bbc.co.uk}}</ref> An early mention of the slogan appeared in a publication called the ''American Magazine'' in 1952 about a trip to Europe''.'' The ''American Magazine'' article stated: "Left pub early because we fly to Paris at 9am. Saw a sign saying 'Take Courage Here.' Learned Courage is a brand of beer."<ref name=":24" />

The slogan was also painted on brewery buildings such as the Anchor Brewery in Southwark <ref>{{Cite web |title=Take Courage, Southwark |url=https://paintedsignsandmosaics.blogspot.com/2010/03/courage.html |access-date=12 May 2025 |website=Painted Signs and Mosaics|date=5 March 2010 }}</ref> and Courage public houses. Many of these remain today as "Ghost Signs".
[[File:Take Courage - geograph.org.uk - 2649003.jpg|left|thumb|Take Courage - Ghost Sign]]
In 2009 Courage's revived the "Take Courage" slogan for a series of posters with the slogan "Take Courage My Friend" as part of a  £2 million advertising campaign.<ref name=":23">{{Cite web |date=15 April 2009 |title=Bottom line gets Dutch Courage advert banned |url=https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/health-fitness/article/bottom-line-gets-dutch-courage-advert-banned-0z0dv27lvpr?region=global |access-date=16 May 2009 |website=thetimes.com}}</ref> The adverts featured men faced with different awkward life situations.

One of the adverts in the series, received a total of three complaints to The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), that the content of the advert implied that drinking a glass of beer would increase the man's confidence in one of the situations depicted. The ASA ruling stated "Although we understood the humorous intention of the scenario, we concluded that the poster breached the code by suggesting that the beer could increase confidence".<ref name=":23" />

The ruling was controversial because of the small number of complaints received to trigger the investigation, leading to the ASA being accused of puritanism. It was also noted that the brewers of Courage at the time, Young's, had been involved in controversy for similar adverts for one of their other beer brands in 2006. The ASA ruling received national news coverage in the United Kingdom which coincidentally increased visibility of the poster which was prominently shown in many of the national newspapers and the BBC website, effectively giving the brewers free advertising and international recognition in Russia, Italy and China among other places. This led to even more controversy.<ref>{{Cite web |date=15 April 2009 |title=Naughty adverts |url=https://boakandbailey.com/2009/04/naughty-adverts/ |access-date=16 May 2025 |website=boakandbailey.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=15 April 2009 |title='Take Courage' beer advert banned |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/7999250.stm |access-date=16 May 2025 |website=news.bbc.co.uk}}</ref><ref name=":24">{{Cite web |last=Cornell |first=Martin |title=Take Courage in the face of idiocy |url=https://zythophile.co.uk/2009/04/18/take-courage-in-the-face-of-idiocy/ |access-date=16 May 2025 |website=zythophile.co.uk|date=18 April 2009 }}</ref>

In the 1970s, Courage's adopted the slogan "It's what your right arms for". The slogan was printed on beer mats including commemorative series such as the Great Engineers Series. Other slogans of the time included "Don't waste valuable Tavern time" and "Courage - In the best tradition".

===TV advertisements===

In the early 1970s, Courage ran a series of TV advertisements that featured bucolic English scenes on sunny summer days with groups of friends taking part in activities such as playing Bowls on Plymouth Hoe or completing a round of golf. The commentary took the form of a poem relaying the sporting activities and successes which were them celebrated in the local pub or club bar ending with the strap-line "A long cool pint of JC".
[[File:Chas & Dave 2015.jpg|left|thumb|Chas & Dave]]
By the end of the 1970s, Courage were looking for a concept for a new set of adverts for Courage Best Bitter and appointed John Webster of BMP to come up with an idea.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=Courage 'gertcha' by Boase Massimi Pollitt Univas |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/courage-gertcha-boase-massimi-pollitt-univas/900879 |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=campaignlive.co.uk}}</ref>  Out one evening for an after work drink with a colleague Webster came across the [[Rockney]] duo [[Chas & Dave]] playing "Woortcha", a song they had written in 1973, in a pub called The Oxford Arms, near Shoreditch and the kernel of an idea for the campaign emerged.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |date=23 October 2007 |title=MORE RABBIT THAN SAINSBURY'S |url=https://recordcollectormag.com/articles/more-rabbit-than-sainsburys |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=recordcollectormag.com}}</ref>

The first advert from the series, "Gertcha" (a remaking of the song "Woortcha") was first aired in 1979. Filmed in black and white, the advert featured an authentic period reconstruction of an East End of London pub from the 1950s.<ref name=":12" /> Coupled with the re-working of Chas & Dave's song, the advert became iconic. The advert rekindled thoughts of Courage's London roots and instantly the word "Gertcha" became commonly used. The advert was nominated for the ITV Award for Advertisements and the British Arrows Awards (British Television Advertising Awards) in 1980.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Courage Best Bitter TV Commercial: Gercha (sic) |url=https://www.hatads.org.uk/catalogue/record/fc8b350a-89ad-4805-b63c-a49821bf8a32 |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=hatads.org.uk}}</ref> The advert proved so popular that it was rerun in 1982.<ref name=":12" /> The advert was placed 85th in the Channel 4 TV programme [[The 100 Greatest TV Ads]] which first aired on 29 April 2000.

The advert propelled Chas & Dave into the limelight with "Gertcha" being released as a single and peaking in the UK music charts at number 20.  Dave Hodges of Chas & Dave has stated that he couldn't walk down the street without someone shouting "Gertcha" at him.<ref name=":13" />

Other [[Chas & Dave]] songs were adapted and used in a series of further adverts based around the same theme, the 1950s East End pub. "[[The Sideboard Song]]", "[[Rabbit (song)|Rabbit]]", "What a miserable Saturday Night", "That's what I like", "[[Margate (song)|Margate]]"  and "Wallop" were all used.<ref>{{cite book |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=uY5KAAAAQBAJ |title=Chas and Dave: All About Us |isbn=9781857828269 |first=Chas |last=Hodges |date=October 2009 |chapter=Chapter 24: No Pleasin' You|publisher=John Blake }}</ref> The advert "Snookered" featuring the Chas & Dave song "Wallop" was nominated for the British Arrows Awards (British Television Advertising Awards) in 1984.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Courage Best Bitter Commercial: Snookered |url=https://www.hatads.org.uk/catalogue/record/e9035b18-e95c-4455-b1fc-715878d986de |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=hatads.org.uk}}</ref>

Most of the TV adverts in the series featured the slogan "Remember a pint of best - Courage do".

===Sponsorship===
====Sports====

The brewery sponsored [[Reading FC]] from 1984 until 1990 reflecting Courage's long term association with the town.<ref>{{cite web |title=Reading – Historical Football Kits |url=http://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Reading/Reading.htm |access-date=2011-05-07 |publisher=Historicalkits.co.uk}}</ref>

Courage sponsored the [[English Premiership (rugby union)|English Premiership]] rugby union league for ten years from 1987 until 1997. Courage were the first sponsors of the league and this was the first club league trophy awarded to a top tier English club. The company logo, the Cockerel, featured in the design of the trophy.  The initial sponsorship was worth £1.6 million for the initial three years. The deal were subsequently renewed for  £2.4 million in 1990. The sponsorship contract was further renewed in 1993  after significant negotiation and an extension of Courage's first refusal arrangements. The sponsorship was worth £7.0 million with an additional marketing and support package worth a further £3.0 million.  Allied Dunbar replaced Courage as league sponsors in 1997 when a new trophy was commissioned.<ref>{{cite web |date=1997-11-01 |title=Rugby Football History |url=http://www.rugbyfootballhistory.com/english%20_league.html |access-date=2011-05-07 |publisher=Rugby Football History}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Meet The Trophies - English Premiership |url=https://worldrugbymuseum.com/from-the-vaults/club-rugby/meet-the-trophies-english-premiership |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=worldrugbymuseum.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Rugby Union: England continue to take Courage: 7m pounds sponsorship |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/rugby-union-england-continue-to-take-courage-7m-pounds-sponsorship-1501115.html |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=independent.co.uk}}</ref>

Courage Best Bitter were an associate club sponsor of [[rugby union]] club the [[Exeter Chiefs]] for the 2011/12 season.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chiefs Sponsors – The home of rugby in Exeter and Devon |url=http://www.exeterchiefs.co.uk/chiefs-sponsors |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903210321/http://www.exeterchiefs.co.uk/chiefs-sponsors |archive-date=2011-09-03 |access-date=2011-05-07 |publisher=Exeterchiefs.co.uk}}</ref>

In 2007, Courage became the official beer for two darts tournaments after signing a deal with the Professional Darts Corporation. The deal saw Courage Best and Directors Bitter stocked at both tournaments and the construction of the "Courage Stand" at the Ladbrokes.com World Championship.<ref>{{Cite web |date=7 November 2007 |title=Official Beer Status For Courage Best |url=https://www.pdc.tv/news/official-beer-status-for-courage-best |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=pdc.tv}}</ref>

====Courage Shire Horse Centre====
[[File:Team of shire horses owned by Thomas Williams, Llwyd Coed Bach, Llanllyfni (1450542).jpg|left|thumb|Shire horses]]
The shire horse is a draught horse which was historically used as a working animal pulling agricultural machinery or delivery carts. The company has always had an affiliation with the shire horses that pulled the beer deliveries through the streets of London. When the limited liability company started in 1888 there were 78 animals stabled at the Anchor Brewhouse. By 1915 the number of horse had increased to 104.<ref name=":25" />

The company took great pride in arranging horses in color. The Courage family, particularly Henry Courage devoted themselves to the horses and delivery teams. Horses were the only means of transport until the company took delivery of its first lorry in January 1916. Even in 1932, the company still had a stable of 32 regular working horses to supplement a fleet of 47 trucks<ref name=":25">{{Cite book |last=Hardinge (Managing Partner 1897–1927) |first=G.S. |title=Courage's 1787–1932 |date=1932 |publisher=Jordan-Gaskell Ltd |location=Victoria, London SW! |pages=22/23 |language=English}}</ref>

The breed fell into decline and faced extinction as their use as working animals was superseded by mechanized automotive power.  In the 1900s there were around a million shire horses in the UK compared to around 3,000 now.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Happened To The Shire Horse Centre? |url=https://great-american-adventures.com/what-happened-to-the-shire-horse-centre/ |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=great-american-adventures.com|date=29 November 2022 }}</ref>

In the mid-1970s Courage began to sponsor a shire horse sanctuary situated in Littlefield Green, near Maidenhead, Berkshire.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |date=15 August 2014 |title=Application to change former Shire Horse Centre into luxury housing estate |url=https://www.maidenhead-advertiser.co.uk/news/26220/Application-to-change-former-Shire-Horse.html |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=Maidenhead Advertiser}}</ref>  The sanctuary provided a home for retired shire horses, together with educating the public about the breed, its history and cultural importance. There was no admission fee.<ref>internet search of Courage Shire Horse Centre Maidenhead</ref> The shire horses and Courage Dray were often seen at fairs and events throughout the local region.

On 5 July 1978, Royal Mail issued postage stamps featuring the Shire Horse to mark the 100th anniversary of the Shire Horse Society. A special commemorative first day cover, featuring the Courage shire horses was commissioned. The first day covers were transported from the Shire Horse Centre to Maidenhead Post Office by shire [[Dray (horse-drawn)|horse-drawn dray]]. The 2 mile journey was completed in 1 1/2 hours.<ref>internet search "Courage Shire Horse First Day Cover 1978"</ref>

The Shire Horse Centre closed in the late 1990s. The site was bought in 2005 and became an animal education center and craft workshop named Village Life. When that closed in 2010, the site became a temporary home for Heroes Berkshire until 2013.<ref name=":14" /> In 2015, the site was purchased by Hicks Development who received planning permission to build 6 large detached properties on the land. The houses are located on a cul-de-sac, called The Shires, adjoining Bath Road ("the A4").<ref name=":14" /><ref>Google Maps research</ref>  The Shire Horse public house is located next to where the entrance to the Courage Shire Horse Centre was located.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Shire Horse |url=https://www.chefandbrewer.com/pubs/berkshire/shire-horse |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=chefandbrewer.com}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
{{in popular culture|date=May 2025}}

Courage Director's Bitter was a favourite of the British television character [[Alan Partridge]]. In the programme, first aired on 25 November 2002, Alan shares this passion during his short-lived friendship with Dan, who states that he has it "''coming out of his taps''" in the episode "Bravealan" (Series 2, Episode 3 of I'm Alan Partridge).<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 November 2002 |title=Bravealan |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0609600/ |access-date=16 May 2025 |website=www.imdb.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Episode 3 – Bravealan |url=https://www.alanpartridgequotes.com/im-alan-partridge/series-2/episode-3-bravealan/ |access-date=20 May 2025 |website=www.alanpartridgequotes.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Alan Partridge's 10 best quotes as he returns for new BBC series This Time |url=https://www.the-independent.com/arts-entertainment/tv/features/alan-partridge-best-quotes-bbc-new-series-show-this-time-steve-coogan-a8795521.html |access-date=20 May 2025 |website=www.the-independent.com}}</ref>

A statue of 'Jacob', a working [[Draft horse|dray horse]], has been placed at the Anchor Brewhouse. The statue commemorates the Courage brewery horses that were stabled beside the establishment, near to where the monument is situated on Queen Elizabeth Street. The stables have long been demolished.<ref>{{Cite web |title=John Courage - (lesser known) monuments featuring animals in London – 10. Jacob the horse… |url=https://exploring-london.com/tag/john-courage/ |access-date=13 May 2025 |website=exploring-london.com|date=19 February 2020 }}</ref>
